questions.question: Under USP <788>, which category of product is expressly exempt from the requirements of this chapter?

options.A: Small-volume injections and suspensions administered by the intramuscular or subcutaneous route
options.C: Large-volume intravenous infusions with a labeled volume above 100 mL
options.D: Small-volume injections containing an emulsion, such as lipid emulsions

questions.explanation: Under <1>, intramuscular or subcutaneous injections must comply with <788>; parenterals intended solely for irrigation and radiopharmaceutical preparations are exempt. Products labeled for use with a final filter may also be exempt where supported by scientific data. Emulsions are not exempt; they may simply need to use the microscopic method instead.

questions.question: A liposomal injection is not clear enough for light obscuration. What does <788> recommend?

options.A: Still use Method 1 and increase the sample volume to compensate
options.B: Waive the particulate test and substitute visual inspection
options.C: Dilute 1:1000 and then use Method 1, with no need to consider Method 2
options.D: Switch to Method 2 (microscopic particle count test); if viscosity is too high, dilute quantitatively before analysis

questions.explanation: Method 1 (light obscuration) is the preferred method, but when a preparation has reduced clarity or increased viscosity (such as emulsions, colloids, and liposomal preparations), or generates air or gas bubbles, Method 2 should be used. If viscosity is too high for either method, the sample can be quantitatively diluted with a suitable diluent.
questions.reference: USP <788> Introduction (Method 1 vs Method 2 applicability paragraph)

questions.question: Before starting light obscuration, the environment and glassware are checked with five 5-mL portions of particle-free water, and the total count of particles of 10 µm and larger is 30 (in 25 mL). How is this judged?

options.A: It exceeds 25 particles, so precautions are inadequate and the preparatory steps must be repeated until the result is acceptable
options.B: It is acceptable, because the total of particles of 10 µm and larger may be as high as 50
options.C: It is acceptable, because the blank test only needs to count particles of 25 µm and larger
options.D: Method 2 must be used to continue testing, without redoing the environment and glassware check

questions.explanation: Five 5-mL portions of particle-free water combined give 25 mL; if more than 25 particles of 10 µm and larger are found, the environment, glassware, or water is inadequately protected, and the preparatory steps must be repeated until the result is acceptable before samples are tested.
questions.reference: USP <788> Method 1 Light Obscuration Particle Count Test › General Precautions

questions.question: A small-volume injection of 5 mL per vial is to be tested by light obscuration. How should the sample be prepared and measured?

options.A: Test each vial individually, take three readings from each, and average all readings as that vial's result
options.B: Pool 3 vials, dilute to 25 mL with particle-free water, and include all four readings
options.C: Pool 10 or more units to at least 25 mL, count four portions of not less than 5 mL each, discard the first, and average the rest
options.D: Pool 10 or more units to 25 mL, count a single 5-mL portion, and discard no readings

questions.explanation: For small-volume injections of less than 25 mL, 10 or more units are pooled to not less than 25 mL (diluted with particle-free water if necessary). Four portions of not less than 5 mL each are then counted for particles of 10 µm and 25 µm and larger; the first result is discarded and the average of the remaining results is calculated. The sample is first mixed by slowly inverting 20 times, and bubbles are allowed to dissipate.
questions.reference: USP <788> Method 1 Light Obscuration Particle Count Test › Method

questions.question: Which set matches the description of the apparatus for Method 2 (microscopic method)?

options.A: Magnification of 400 ± 10, gridded white filter, nominal pore size 5 µm, a single vertical light source, no oblique illumination
options.B: Magnification of 100 ± 10, black or dark gray filter with nominal pore size 1.0 µm or finer, bright-field illumination plus oblique illumination at 10°–20°
options.C: Magnification of 100 ± 10, gridded white filter, nominal pore size 5 µm, only 10°–20° oblique illumination needed, counting in a radial pattern
options.D: Magnification of 40 ± 10, filter of any color, any pore size, a single built-in light source, no auxiliary illumination needed

questions.explanation: Method 2 uses a binocular microscope at 100 ± 10 magnification, with a black or dark gray filter (gridded or not) with a nominal pore size of 1.0 µm or finer; two illuminators are needed: episcopic bright-field illumination within the microscope, and an external auxiliary illuminator adjustable to give reflected oblique light at 10°–20°.
questions.reference: USP <788> Method 2 Microscopic Particle Count Test (apparatus description)

questions.topic: Test 1.A limits applied to an LVP
questions.question: A 500-mL infusion solution is tested by light obscuration and averages 20 particles/mL of ≥10 µm and 4 particles/mL of ≥25 µm. What is the outcome?

options.A: It complies, because the ≥10 µm count is below 25 particles/mL and ≥25 µm is relaxed separately
options.B: It complies, because Test 1.A limits only particles of ≥10 µm, ≥25 µm is for information only, and the ≥25 µm limit is separately relaxed to 10 particles/mL
options.C: It does not meet the Method 1 criteria, because ≥25 µm exceeds 3 particles/mL; retest by Method 2
options.D: It does not comply, and it may not be retested by Method 2 or any other method; the batch is rejected outright

questions.explanation: Test 1.A applies to containers with a labeled volume above 100 mL: the average must not exceed 25 particles/mL (≥10 µm) and 3 particles/mL (≥25 µm). Both limits must be met, and 4 particles/mL at ≥25 µm already exceeds the limit; when the average is exceeded, the microscopic particle count test should be performed.

questions.question: An injection with a labeled volume of exactly 100 mL is tested by light obscuration. Which set of criteria applies?

options.A: Test 1.B: not more than 6000 particles of ≥10 µm and 600 particles of ≥25 µm per container
options.B: Test 1.A: not more than 25 particles of ≥10 µm and 3 particles of ≥25 µm per mL
options.C: Test 1.B: not more than 3000 particles of ≥10 µm and 300 particles of ≥25 µm per container
options.D: Test 1.A: not more than 6000 particles of ≥10 µm and 600 particles of ≥25 µm per container

questions.explanation: Test 1.A applies only to a labeled volume above 100 mL; volumes of 100 mL or less (including exactly 100 mL) use Test 1.B, with limits of 6000 particles (≥10 µm) and 600 particles (≥25 µm) per container. The 3000/300 limits belong to Test 2.B of the microscopic method.

questions.question: For an infusion solution with a labeled volume above 100 mL tested by the microscopic method, what are the Test 2.A limits?

options.A: Not more than 25 particles of ≥10 µm and 3 particles of ≥25 µm per mL
options.B: Not more than 3000 particles of ≥10 µm and 300 particles of ≥25 µm per container
options.C: Not more than 6000 particles of ≥10 µm and 600 particles of ≥25 µm per container
options.D: Not more than 12 particles of ≥10 µm and 2 particles of ≥25 µm per mL

questions.explanation: For containers above 100 mL, the microscopic method uses Test 2.A: the average must not exceed 12 particles/mL (≥10 µm) and 2 particles/mL (≥25 µm), which is stricter than light obscuration Test 1.A (25 and 3 particles/mL). The "25 and 3 particles per mL" limits belong to light obscuration, and the "3000 and 300 per container" limits are those of the microscopic method for containers of 100 mL or less.

questions.question: A pharmacy bulk package labeled "Not for Direct Infusion" has a total volume of 100 mL and a labeled maximum dose volume of 10 mL. The average count is 50 particles of ≥10 µm per mL. What is the converted test result?

options.A: 50 particles, using the per-mL average directly without any conversion
options.B: 5 particles, dividing the per-mL average by the maximum dose volume of 10 mL
options.C: 500 particles, calculated for the portion equal to the 10-mL maximum dose and treated as one container
options.D: 5000 particles, calculated from the total 100-mL package volume and treated as one container

questions.explanation: Pharmacy bulk packages of 25 mL or more are tested as small-volume injections, with the result calculated for the portion equivalent to the labeled maximum dose: the per-mL average multiplied by 10 mL gives 500 particles, treated as the contents of one complete container and compared with the limits.
questions.reference: USP <788> Method 1 › Method (pharmacy bulk packages paragraph)

questions.question: A dual-compartment package (drug in one chamber, diluent in the other) is to be tested for particulate matter. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Prepare it as a large- or small-volume injection according to container volume; activate and shake as labeled to mix and dissolve the components before testing
options.B: Always treat it as a small-volume injection regardless of container volume, without first mixing the contents of the two chambers
options.C: Test the two chambers separately, each prepared according to its own volume, without activating or mixing before testing
options.D: Dual-compartment packages are exempt from <788> because they contain a diluent, so no particulate test is needed

questions.explanation: Dual-compartment packages are prepared and tested as large- or small-volume injections according to container volume; before testing they must be activated and shaken as labeled so that the components are well mixed and the drug is dissolved. The chapter lists only specific exemptions, and dual-compartment packages are not among them.
